Opening day: the cafeteria ran out of rice by eleven, and three ministers blamed each other.
Opening weeks. Half the new members are still looking for their offices; the other half are looking for the exit.
The new members' table is the loudest in the room. It won't be by winter.
Chestnut rice is back on the menu, and so is the old argument about whose district grows the best chestnuts.
Boots are steaming by the radiators. The talk is snowplough budgets, as it is every year.
Someone has put cherry branches on every table. The Environment committee wants to know whose orchard they came from.
The air conditioning is broken again. Government Administration is suddenly very interested in procurement.
Since the Fisheries Quota Act passed, the Agriculture committee's table eats in silence.
The fisheries lobbyist is eating alone. The Quota Act's defeat cost her a lot of lunches.
The cashier explains the new consumption tax at every till. Nobody thanks the Committee on Finance.
The Tomari restart passed. The Environment committee has moved its table to the far corner.
The Integrated Resort Act passed. Three members are already arguing about who cuts the ribbon.
Since the Donation Transparency Act, nobody pays for anyone's lunch. Receipts are everywhere.
A priest came by to thank the heritage committee in person. He brought sweets for the whole table.
The Shinkansen members are drawing station maps on napkins again.
Rural doctors write to members by name since the hospital network passed. Some of the letters are thank-yous.
Two staffers are comparing parental leave forms. One of them has already filled his in.
The Carbon Levy's defeat hangs over the Environment table. Someone has left a single paper cup on it, pointedly.

speaker: colleague
text: A colleague slides into the seat beside you. "The leadership likes you this week. Enjoy it."
Your party's table goes quiet when you sit down. Someone remembers an urgent call.
A delegation in matching jackets photographs the fountain, then the guards, then each other.
Two lobbyists pass on the path, nod, and both turn to watch where the other goes.
A university group is rehearsing chants quietly behind the hedge.
A man in waders waits by the gate. Someone from the harbor towns, by the look of the boots.
A minister's car idles at the side entrance. The driver has been told to keep the engine running.
A tour guide explains the Assembly's history with more confidence than accuracy.
Three monks walk the gravel path slowly, as if counting the steps.
A camera crew sets up by the pond and waits for anyone famous to look unhappy.
A farmers' delegation carries a sack of rice to the front steps. Security debates whether rice is a protest.
An aide paces the rose beds rehearsing a speech under her breath. She stumbles on the same word every time.
Two members from rival parties share a bench and pretend not to know each other.
A businessman checks his watch, then the main doors, then his watch again. Someone is late for him.
A child on a school trip asks the guard whether Parliament has a gift shop. It does not.
Workers in hard hats are measuring the east wall. Nobody seems to know which committee ordered it.
An Ainu elder stops at the memorial stone and stays a long time.
A courier on a bicycle drops a thick envelope at the desk and leaves before anyone can sign for it.
Banners from the Tomari vote are still tied to the railings, faded now.
The gardeners have wrapped the pines in straw. The members haven't noticed; the gardeners don't mind.
Visitors crowd the cherry trees. Inside, the session runs late and nobody sees them.
New members walk the gardens with maps. By winter they'll take the shortcut through the kitchens.
The whispers speak of nothing new.
The rumor mill is on the same subjects as before.
Idle chatter. Nothing worth hearing.
A mix of dialects and languages flows through the air.
After some time all the chatter becomes noise.
The same three rumors, told a fourth time.
Someone is retelling yesterday's gossip with new adjectives.
The talk has drifted to the weather and the price of parking.
Nothing here you haven't heard already.
The tables are arguing about baseball now.
Every story ends with "but you didn't hear it from me", and you already had.
The gossip has gone stale, like the afternoon tea.
Even the rumors are repeating themselves.
A long story about a ministry printer. You've heard it.
The room is talking, but not about anything new.
Old news, warmed over.
The whisper network is taking a break.
Someone is quoting a rumor back to the person who started it.
The chatter circles back to where it began.
Nothing worth repeating. You've listened twice.
